# Incorta 4.0 — A Tale of 2 Apps

## It took 2.5 years, 3 iterations, 4 product release proposals, and a whole lot of patience. But it’s finally here.

[![Ahmad Badr](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/1*5leT3MrY9LBqjxySxsGwNg.jpeg)](https://medium.com/@ahmad.ihab.badr?source=post_page---byline--92ca64dafaf5-----------------------------------------)

Incorta is the industry’s first hyper-converged analytics tool (more on that [here](http://www.incorta.com/)). In 2016, its web application, the primary medium through which customers harnessed Incorta’s power, was reaching a dire state.

The app interface, designed initially as an iPad app and then roughly cut and paste to work on the web, was riddled with design inconsistencies and strange interaction patterns carried over from the iPad days.

Its fledgling codebase, built in Angular 1, could no longer handle the growing business requirements nor support complex flows. New features were hacked into workable shape to minimize the damage.

The situation was precarious.

Press enter or click to view image in full size![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:574/1*ST5ZHlrrwPBunZXQctdf6g.jpeg)

Press enter or click to view image in full size![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:2102/1*bjS_Ch-_WXLcHK6KH400qw.png)

Incorta in 2016 (left). Incorta in 2018 (right).

Fast forward to 2018! Incorta 4.0 has just been released, bringing with it a completely redesigned experience and re-engineered codebase (React).

One screenshot won’t do the full journey justice. In the following brief, I’ll discuss how we got to this point and the challenges we faced along the way.

### 1\. Why did we redesign and who were we designing for?

We started out with a series of interviews with stakeholders. This gave us a list of the **business requirements**:

- provide a flexible UI framework that would accommodate future changes and expansion
- give Incorta, which is an enterprise app, a consumer-grade experience
- help the front-end team transition from Angular to React

We then set about understanding our users. We conducted on-site research sessions that enabled us to create three loose personas:

1. _Developers—_ connected to databases, maintained data integrity and relationships, and handed datasets off to…
2. _Analysts —_ utilized data provided by developers to create reports and dashboards and then shared them with…
3. _Consumers —_ received dashboards and used them to answer day to day business questions related to sales, marketing, manufacturing, etc…

Consumers accounted for the majority of our users.

### **2\. What were the primary issues all of our users faced?**

Further investigation with customers, along with our support and technical sales teams helped us hone in on 3 primary issues:

- _Untrustworthy UI —_ users found our primary color ‘childish’ and associated Incorta with ‘instability’ and ‘risk’. The interaction patterns carried over from the iPad days, poorly written copy, and the occasional bug compounded these negative perceptions.

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:303/1*0HiFDN7zRFvPdjRm-YRoIA.png)

Filters are a good example of the interaction patterns carried from the iPad. Note the actions on the top, and the operator (in the center) and list of filter categories that opened their own respective pages.

- _Lack of Feedback—_ many areas of the application lacked basic feedback mechanisms, such as a success notification after saving or updating a page.
- _Lack of Guidance —_ users complained about having a hard time understanding how features worked. Documentation was present, but there was nothing in the app itself that guided to it (plus most users didn’t read documentation).

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:640/1*XkIgmAfVeyt8Q2gkHyzJWg.jpeg)

When editing the dashboard layout, most users (myself included) had no idea that you could press the highlighted icon to copy a report and then paste it into another dashboard.

### 3\. Ok, we knew what the problems were, but how did we plan to tackle this project?

The primary question that delayed the project was related to product strategy: how do we build the new app without putting existing commitments on hold? There were 4 models proposed: 2 advocated for a ‘Separation Model’ and 2 for a ‘Hybrid Model’.

_Separation Models_

1. Build an entirely new app and completely get rid of the old one
2. Build the new app in pieces and run both old and new apps simultaneously, allowing users to switch back and forth

Press enter or click to view image in full size![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1600/1*j4ur-GwnGT9v-AP2NdoVaw.png)

Press enter or click to view image in full size![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1600/1*7527ERUulIN0H99J0EprZg.png)

Salesforce utilized the second model. Users could switch back and forth between the old and new experiences, however, after testing a prototype, the feedback was that the experience felt janky and disconnected.

_Hybrid Models_

1. Systematically build the new app from inside the old one (i.e. React built on Angular)
2. Systematically deprecate the old app from inside the new one (i.e. Angular embedded in React). **We decided to move with this proposal.** It was easier to develop, reduced the risk of project delays, and provided a smoother experience.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1000/1*8vOlPqLaY5MRNBA2YY8Wug.png)

An early wireframe demonstrating how we’d embedded the old app (right) into the new one (left).

We opted to focus on the consumer-user experience first, given that they represented our largest user base. We built those redesigned experiences in React and scheduled the rest for deprecation and redesign in later releases.

### 4\. How did we address the high level user issues?

We broke down the aforementioned issues into smaller pieces, and addressed them in the following manner:

- _Visual—_ we utilized color theory to select a new primary color that instilled a sense of stability and security. The supporting palette included a lot of toned-down colors so as not to distract from the content.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*sjlf9Jm1LSXmCpEDP-n22w.jpeg)

The new color palette.

- _Interaction patterns —_ we redesigned components so that they were a) modular & re-usable and b) web-based.Our front-end team utilized the [Ant Design](https://ant.design/) UI framework to speed up development.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*sc2l3gsWlG41sfRS9GLpHw.png)

The redesigned filtering experience. This was a combination of AntD components (e.g: search, dropdown, and multi-select) and custom components.

- _Enhanced UX Copy—_ we took the opportunity to revisit our copy, targeting a consistent tense that was friendly, helpful, and succinct in every context.

Press enter or click to view image in full size![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:362/1*4ldI9coxiWXn_5_FFLnjEQ.png)

Press enter or click to view image in full size![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:2420/1*6Wth9sjRQosM8gy5nczXpw.png)

Menu labels started with a verb and were written in title cases (left). Our 404 page was both friendly at a time where users could be frustrated, and helpful, guiding them out of the problem (right).

- _Feedback Loops —_ we set about identifying areas where the application could do a better job of giving feedback, and created a preliminary feedback style-guide that included voice, tense, and style.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*txPSzqII3A6J7o1nnCAkZw.jpeg)

In this example, there are 3 potential success scenarios when sharing a dashboard. Each of them follow the same tense (past), voice (passive in title, active in body), and styling (navigable names are hyper-linked).

- _In-App Guidance —_ we inserted guiding micro-copy on empty screens, modals, and other components. Depending on the context, we would either expose it or hide it behind an info/help icon.

Press enter or click to view image in full size![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:2412/1*kVpauxLLbt9UAaM5fUCL2Q.png)

Press enter or click to view image in full size![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1334/1*qAAOdrbH4HsQ-uoK1IyIsA.png)

If no widget is selected, the ‘action-bar’ on the ‘Edit Layout’ page helps users understand what actions they can take (left). CTA’s were inserted on empty screens (pop-overs, modals, and pages), guiding users to the appropriate action (right).

### 5\. How did we ensure we were on the right track?

We validated our ideas using prototypes, video demos, customer 1–1s, presentations, and guerrilla usability tests . At every decision point, we wanted to make sure we were investing effort in the right direction (despite our best efforts, one idea did slip through the cracks, which you can read about [here](https://medium.com/@ahmad.ihab.badr/how-to-take-an-idea-from-feature-to-failure-b1a867f5236c)).

Press enter or click to view image in full size![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1920/1*c8TiXgAUV45xlFy7K8wPUw.gif)

Press enter or click to view image in full size![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:3360/1*rZXmXd3iiq7ratwEzUy_tA.gif)

Early-stage exploration of a ‘layout-editing’ interaction (left). Later-stage prototype for a filtering concept that was discarded after internal usability testing demonstrated users struggled with the ‘moving’ search.

In order to manage feedback from outside sources (i.e. not collected by the product team), we created two channels on Slack: #ux40\_bugs and #ux40\_feedback, that served as our central ‘feedback repositories’.

These channels also gave us a platform to run guerrilla usability tests, sanity checks, or discuss explorations and upcoming features with the broader team.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*6LH6MqlWPIxI92nMUEB7zA.png)

Slack channels instilled ownership in employees and enabled frequent discussions around feedback.

Customer Success, Support, and Implementation teams would raise issues or applaud easter-eggs they found or that external users shared; QA, Engineering, and Marketing would discuss whether they thought they’d found a bug or share thoughts about how to take the product to the next level.

Soliciting company feedback and giving co-workers a platform that empowered them to contribute and feel ownership across two continents was just as challenging as getting this project out.

### 6\. How did we do?

From a business perspective, we achieved our goals:we were now fully on our way to deprecating Angular and working in React, the new UI framework was flexible enough to handle the steady flow of features and requests, and the UX changes pushed us further towards our goal of a consumer-grade experience.

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:320/1*RCqb8bMZtF0pX_C4GoIVUg.png)

React (Source: [Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/React-icon.svg/320px-React-icon.svg.png))

Research sessions and feedback received post-release revealed the following user perceptions of the the redesign (internal, customers, and prospects):

- the application was easier to navigate and discover
- the interface (primarily the dashboard page) was now comparable to if not better than competitors on the market and felt more ‘familiar’
- the attentiveness to detail was appreciated and considered a sign of product advancement and maturity

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*6F_VQaRYuqp_BZrVNpdrhw.png)

Clicking on table cells now affords users the opportunity to select between several actions, whereas previously, clicking would automatically perform the latter option.

Having completed the first phase of this project, we set about planning the next section of the application to deprecate as well as prioritizing bugs and enhancements for the next release.

Getting to this point was no easy feat. It involved aligning goals across multiple teams, several iterations and failures, and lots of patient planning. We’re proud of where we’ve gotten to today and are excited for the future!
